pages.headline: **386 five-star reviews** say she is Tulsa's insurance-claim roofer. Her website says “quality roofing.”
pages.dek: Homeowners already chose Marisol Vega for one job: getting a hail claim paid and the roof replaced. The proof is everywhere except where buyers decide. This audit shows what a buyer's diligence finds first, scores the brand on ten checked rows, and hands agents a dated plan to turn that proof into inspection calls before spring hail season.

pages.headline: Eight things the evidence says that you would **not guess** from her profiles
pages.dek: Each finding pairs a checked fact with what it changes and the action that follows. Seven are observed directly; one is a measurement gap that blocks proving any result.

items.title: 236 of 386 reviews describe an insurance claim. The homepage never says it.
items.body: Customers already decided what she is: 61% of her 4.9-star Google reviews mention an adjuster, a claim or insurance, and 104 name Marisol herself. The site leads with “Quality roofing you can trust” — a line any roofer could use — while the top three competitors lead with hail and claims.
items.so: Rename the offer to what buyers already buy: insurance-claim roof replacement, led by Marisol.

items.title: Her best video has 41,200 views. Her website has 0 videos.
items.body: Five storm-prep and hail-claim videos hold 88,650 views while the other 207 have a median of 160. None of the 41 site pages embeds one, and no page explains the claim process that the top video already teaches step by step.
items.so: The claim guide already exists on camera; publish it as the site's main page and let the video sell.

items.title: 3 of 4 ways to reach her fail: form, financing and tap-to-call.
items.body: The menu links /financing on all 41 pages and it returns 404. The contact form posts to an address on a domain that expired in January 2025, so form leads since then may never have arrived. On mobile the phone number is an image and cannot be tapped.
items.so: Before any spend, fix the three doors and prove each with a real test submission.

items.title: Search her name: the first 6 results are a realtor and an actress.
items.body: For the bare name a Miami realtor holds #1-#3 and an actress #4-#6; the founder appears at #7. Add “roofing” and she owns the top three. Asked “who is Marisol Vega roofing,” 1 of 3 AI engines described the realtor instead.
items.so: Every page and profile should carry the qualifier “Marisol Vega, Tulsa roofer” and one Person record machines can read.

items.title: A TV segment, a 2025 award and an expo talk — 0 point home.
items.body: Green Country News 6 (April 2024) and the 2025 Women in Roofing award both link to a Facebook page silent since February 2023, under the old name “Vega Roof Pros.” The site never mentions the segment, the award, the podcast or the talk.
items.so: Ask both publishers to relink and add an “As seen on” block, so independent proof lands where buyers decide.

items.title: AI engines named her once in 3 answers and cited 0 of her pages.
items.body: Asked for the best Tulsa roofer for hail damage, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity each named 3-5 firms; Vega appeared once, fourth. Every cited source was a listicle, a BBB page or a competitor — engines cannot quote a claim guide that does not exist yet.
items.so: Publish the claim guide and a dated facts page — the two pages an AI answer would quote.

items.title: 3 names, 2 founding years and 2 roof counts split her proof.
items.body: Google says “Vega Roofing LLC,” the site “Vega Roofing & Restoration,” Facebook and LinkedIn “Vega Roof Pros.” The founding year is 2010 on the site and 2012 on Google; roofs are “3,500+” on the homepage and “more than 2,000” in the 2024 interview.
items.so: Choose one public name and one set of dated facts, then correct every profile in the same week.

items.title: 0 conversions are tracked, so no one can say which channel books inspections.
items.body: GA4 is installed with zero conversion events and there is no call-tracking number. The goal — 30% more inspection calls before spring — cannot be measured from today's setup, and lead volume and close rate by source are unknown.
items.so: Install call tracking and two GA4 events this week so spring's results are counted, not guessed.

text: Why the insurance angle and not price: the owner reports roughly 70% of revenue already comes from insurance jobs, and reviews name the claim help far more often than speed or cost. Competitors that rank 1-3 for “roof repair tulsa” lead with hail and claims, so “quality roofing” is not a differentiator in this market — it is the default. The fastest credible lift is to say plainly what customers already say about her.

items.body: Only 22 of 386 reviews mention price or financing; 236 mention the claim. Buyers who arrive through the claim story compare on trust, which is where her proof is strongest.
items.so: Keep financing one click away, not on the hero.

blocks.body: The expo photo with the national influencer is co-presence, not an endorsement — it must not appear as a testimonial. Dana Whitfield's 7 joint appearances support a proposed claim-guide partnership, which needs her consent before any public use of her name.

text: How to use each tie, in order: Dana Whitfield first, because seven joint appearances already exist and a co-branded claim guide gives both of them something they cannot build alone. News 6 second, because one relink email turns a 2024 segment into a permanent proof link. The manufacturer third, because its locator page is where homeowners compare certified installers — and her listing has no photos. The softball league last: real community proof, low buyer relevance.
What not to do: tag the national influencer, quote him, or crop the expo photo into a testimonial. One shared photo from 2025 supports nothing beyond “both attended.”

blocks.title: Spend gate
blocks.body: No live spend, audience change or scaling without Marisol's approval of the exact account, budget, dates and metric. The day-7 read is a decision point, not an automatic step.

text: How to read day 7: the test passes if the paid video earns 15-second views at or below the organic channel's cost-equivalent and produces at least one tracked call. It fails if cost per 15-second view is more than double the baseline or no tracked call arrives. A pass earns $30 over 30 days; a fail sends the creative back to Process, not to a bigger budget. Every number comes from the ad account and A12's tracking — none from estimates.
